newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Cronenberg courts controversy anew with "Crash".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cronenberg courts controversy anew with "Crash".

text.p: David Cronenberg, whose films about mutating scientists, killer dwarves and malevolent gynecologists have shocked movie audiences, expects his latest movie to have a similar impact.

But the award-winning Canadian director said "Crash," about people who are erotically obsessed with car crashes, should not be judged by the critical standards applied to most movies. "I think you really have to leave your normal critical faculties at home because it doesn't work like most movies," he told Reuters. "If you try to plug your own normal responses into the film they just won't fit."

"Crash," which stars Holly Hunter, James Spader and Rosanna Arquette, has already attracted a storm of controversy. It was both booed and cheered by audiences at its debut at the Cannes film festival, where it won a special prize for "audacity, daring and originality."

But the movie reportedly caused a deep rift in the jury, with two members abstaining from the final vote. Critics have also been sharply divided. Some label the movie pornographic for its graphic and frequent depiction of car-related sex. Others hail it as brilliant.

With the movie now in theatres in Canada and soon to be released worldwide, Cronenberg said he expects "Crash" to receive a similar response from the general public. "It will continue to split audiences. I think there will be people who walk out of every screening," he predicted.

"Crash" is based on the 1973 cult novel of the same name by British science fiction writer J.G. Ballard, which tells the story of a group of people who are erotically aroused by car accidents and anything related to them.

Cronenberg said he was repelled by the novel's dark vision when he first read it but could never get it out of his head. He said he felt compelled to make the book into a movie for reasons he is only now beginning to understand.

"You never know when something is going to choose you. Basically the book chose me. When I read it, I couldn't say I really liked it," he said. "I really put it down thinking there is no way I would make this into a movie."

The director now sees "Crash" as a "strange existentialist romance," which examines the way people are now redefining love, sexuality and the nature of relationships. He said the characters' experiences in the film at some level relate to what happens in everyone's life.

Cronenberg, who directed such critically acclaimed films as "The Fly," "Dead Ringers" and "Naked Lunch," is no stranger to controversial subject matter. His first feature, "Shivers," a low-budget horror film, was denounced in Canada's parliament in the 1970s. But Cronenberg has since earned a reputation as a gifted director who turns horror into high art.

As a result, movie stars like Briton Jeremy Irons have flocked to work with the Toronto-based director. The all-star cast of "Crash" worked for less than their normal pay to keep the budget to a relatively low $9 million, Cronenberg said.
He believes actors such as Holly Hunter and Rosanna Arquette are drawn to work with him because his films differ from Hollywood's commercial mainstream fare.

"Certain kinds of actors see a kindred spirit of adventure and danger and not wanting to play it safe. Actors can get very bored with themselves if they feel like they're doing the same role over and over again," Cronenberg said. "I'm providing them with roles that they've never seen before."

One criticism of his work that Cronenberg finds hard to accept is that his films are a deliberate attempt to shock. The soft-spoken, mild-mannered director hardly seems the kind of personality who would make films to horrify and offend.

"I don't think of myself as a confrontational film maker. Some people say 'Why do you need to shock people?' I don't need to shock people. I think maybe somebody like Oliver Stone does need to shock people. He is an aggressive, combative guy. I'm not that."

Cronenberg admits he did expect, and continues to expect, his film to provoke a strong -- if mixed -- reaction from audiences worldwide. "You can't expect to make a movie honestly of a book like "Crash" and not have it be controversial because the book was so controversial," he said.
"There is a satisfaction really in getting the response that you thought you would get."
